message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure, Harbourside Hotel

The arithmetic in the document checks out, and the competitor comparison is accurate. However, the key claims in your description don't hold up against the document's own data:
- The price-sensitivity "test" is confounded by seasonality.
- The £204,000 is a ceiling built on an overstated room count, not a floor.
- The two-night minimum is likely to clash directly with the 38% of Saturday business that comes from weddings.

## Major issues

### 1. The price test is confounded by seasonality

The case rests on occupancy rising from 81% in June to 89% in July after the £10 increase. Table 1 shows why that tells you nothing about price:

> May 85% | **Jun 81%** | **Jul 89%** | **Aug 93%** | Sep 88%

- July and August are peak months by the document's own account, driven by the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would have risen in July at any price.
- June's 81% is itself a dip below May's 85%, so the starting point is unusually low.
- The rise came in the **last week of June**. Weekend leisure stays are booked weeks ahead, so many July guests probably booked at £135 before the increase took effect.
- A valid test would compare July 2025 with July 2024 at a similar rate, or compare pick-up for bookings made after the change.

As it stands, the evidence neither shows that guests are price-insensitive nor that the higher rate "reinforced our positioning."

### 2. The £204,000 is overstated, and it's a ceiling, not a floor

**Room count.** Section 2 says the hotel has **112** rooms. Section 5 uses **124**.

| | Rooms × 104 nights × 79% × £20 |
|---|---|
| As written (124 rooms) | **£203,800** |
| Correct (112 rooms) | **£184,000** |

**Not every booking is at BAR.** The £20 applies only to BAR bookings, but the document exempts corporate contracts and contracted group rates. Weddings alone account for about 38% of Saturday room bookings, booked as blocks through the couple. If those blocks make up roughly a fifth of all weekend room-nights, the uplift falls to about **£150,000**. It falls further once packages, other discounted rates and OTA commission are deducted.

**"Assumes no occupancy gain."** That's true, but it's not what makes an estimate conservative. The real risk is occupancy *loss*, and the model assumes none. Assuming that volume holds after a 14% price rise is the optimistic case, not the prudent one.

**The minimum-stay revenue may be negative.** Leaving it unquantified doesn't make the estimate conservative if the effect could be a loss (see point 3).

### 3. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business

Section 4 sets out both sides of the problem without connecting them:
- About 38% of Saturday bookings are wedding guests who arrive on Saturday and leave on Sunday, which are exactly the one-night stays the minimum blocks.
- Future wedding blocks that haven't yet been contracted would fall under the rule. Couples may steer guests elsewhere, and Quayside Hall may start recommending other hotels. That puts a key relationship at risk.

**The minimum only pays when Saturday would sell out anyway.**
- The hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays. On the other 21, the minimum turns away one-night guests the hotel would otherwise have taken.
- The document expects the gain "particularly in shoulder months." Those are precisely the months least likely to sell out, so that's where the minimum is most likely to *cost* revenue.

At minimum, the policy should apply only to dates forecast to sell out, with wedding blocks exempt.

### 4. The "value" position changes after the rise

- Competitors charge £165 to £180. At £165, Harbourside would no longer be £20 to £35 cheaper. It would match the cheapest hotel in the set.
- The 8.4 value-for-money score was earned at the lowest price in the set. It's evidence the current price works, not that guests will accept a higher one. The rise is likely to erode the very advantage being cited.

## Smaller issues

- **Monitoring trigger.**
  - Weekend leisure stays are booked well ahead. By the time a full month of occupancy falls five points, the following months are already booked at that lower level.
  - Weekly pick-up against 2025 is the better early signal. The trigger should be set on pick-up, not on achieved occupancy.
  - It would also help to track RevPAR and food-and-beverage spend, not occupancy alone.
- **Headroom is worth stating.** Revenue per available weekend room is currently £145 × 79% ≈ £114.55. At £165, occupancy can fall to about 69% before room revenue is lower than today, a cushion of roughly 10 points. That's the honest measure of risk, and it's reasonably reassuring. It belongs in the paper.
- **First-year timing.** Many June and July 2026 stays will already be booked at £145 by 15 May, so first-year revenue will fall short of a full-year figure.
- **Recommendation wording.** "Delivering at least £204,000" should not survive the corrections above.

## What holds up

- 52 weekends × 2 nights = 104 nights, and the 2025 average occupancy is 79.2%. Both are correct.
- The competitor gap of £20 to £35 is accurate at current rates.
- Saturday is genuinely constrained, and 31 sell-outs is a real signal that there's pricing power on peak dates.

## Suggested revisions

1. Fix the room count (112) and restate revenue for BAR bookings only, net of commission, as a range.
2. Replace the June–July comparison with a year-on-year or booking-date analysis, or drop it.
3. Add a break-even occupancy figure (about 69%) and model a few volume-loss scenarios.
4. Restrict the two-night minimum to forecast sell-out dates, exempt wedding blocks, and talk to Quayside Hall first.
5. Base the monitoring trigger on weekly pick-up and RevPAR, not monthly occupancy.

A rate increase is plausibly justified: Harbourside is at the bottom of its set and sells out often. But the current paper doesn't establish that it is low-risk, and it overstates the gain by at least £20,000 before the other adjustments.
